text: Do you know engineers saved the Leaning Tower of Pisa by digging soil out from under it?
It's fifty-six metres of white marble, and its top leans almost four metres out of line.
The problem is underneath. Its foundation is only three metres deep, set in weak, unstable ground.
Building began in eleven seventy-three. Five years later, as the second floor went up, one side was already sinking.
Then war stopped the work for almost a century. That pause saved it. The soil underneath had time to settle.
When building restarted, the upper floors were made taller on one side, to make up for the tilt. So the tower isn't straight. It's curved.
But the lean kept growing, century after century. In nineteen ninety, the tower was closed to the public.
First, engineers stacked eight hundred and seventy tonnes of lead at its base, on the high side.
Steel cables were looped around the third level and anchored far away, to hold it safe.
Then came the clever part. Long drills, slanted under the high side, pulled out the soil, a little at a time.
Thirty-eight cubic metres in all. As the ground closed in, the high side slowly sank.
And the tower eased back by forty-five centimetres, to where it stood in eighteen thirty-eight.
It reopened in two thousand and one, and engineers expect it to stay stable for at least three hundred years.
